Cross-Border Transmission Regimes: ANOVA and Cluster Analysis

Statistical validation of the transmission-regime taxonomy in the LEEDS MRIO-SFC model

Author

Oriol Vallès Codina

October 2, 2026

1 Introduction

This report statistically validates the five transmission-regime taxonomy used in the LEEDS MRIO-SFC model analysis of circular economy (CE) transition scenarios. The taxonomy classifies 14 CE scenarios into five groups based on their cross-border spillover mechanism:

Regime Scenarios Mechanism
Production Leakage Sc1, 4, 9 Secondary sector’s higher import content unintentionally raises RoW intermediate exports
Symmetric Contraction Sc3, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12 Both regions contract proportionally; EU restructuring generates no directional asymmetry
Competitive Displacement Sc10 Secondary metals’ lower A-matrix row-sum frees EU intermediate resources; only scenario with true sign reversal (EU↑, RoW↓)
Fossil Import Collapse Sc2, 13 EU fossil import reduction collapses RoW hydrocarbon export revenues; RoW fiscal space deteriorates
Construction Rebound Sc5, 14 Investment channel dominates; CE policy raises fixed investment, reversing ecological sign

The analysis proceeds in four stages. First, the long-term (t+20) percentage deviation from baseline is computed for each region separately, for an extended set of 34 documented aggregates across all 14 scenarios; the EU−RoW divergence Z1 − Z2 is formed from these, and the joint (Z1, Z2) profile is retained alongside it. Second, a one-way ANOVA tests whether mean divergences differ significantly across regimes for each variable, measuring the effect size with η². Third, hierarchical clustering (Ward’s D2 linkage, Euclidean distance on standardised profiles) is run in both coordinate spaces, and the presence of cluster structure is tested against a permutation null rather than against the gap statistic or a Gaussian mixture model, both of which are unidentified at p/n ≈ 2.4. Fourth, because the number of clusters is not identified at n=14, the paper’s five-regime taxonomy is treated as a hypothesis specified in advance and scored against the data with the adjusted Rand index, block by block, to establish which variables carry the regime signal.

The 23 core variables from the shock-summary tables are supplemented with 14 additional documented aggregates: disposable income decomposition (yd, ydw, ydc), functional inequality (ineq), the debt-to-GDP ratio, wage bill, corporate profit, cumulative CO₂ concentration, trade flows (imp, rex), fiscal flows (g, t), and output aggregates (y, fd). Variables with zero variance in their Z1−Z2 divergence are excluded from clustering (accounting identities such as current account and trade balance cancel bilaterally).

3 EU−RoW Divergence Heatmap

Discussion. The heatmap reveals an immediately striking structural feature: the vast majority of cells are near-zero (white), with intense coloration concentrated in only two regime blocks — Fossil Import Collapse and Construction Rebound. This reflects the fundamental asymmetry of the scenario set: most CE interventions operate within small-scale material substitutions that generate proportional bilateral adjustments, while energy and construction transitions operate through qualitatively different channels.

Why energy (Sc2, Sc13) is so intense. The Fossil Import Collapse regime generates the deepest red cells in the ecological columns — emissions (−1.53, Sc13) — indicating that RoW’s ecological footprint deteriorates far more than EU’s in the carbon dimension. The land and water divergences for Sc13 are an order of magnitude smaller (+0.17 and −0.03 respectively): the fossil-import channel is an emissions channel, not a land or water one. The mechanism is the import substitution channel: EU households and firms reducing fossil fuel purchases shift spending toward domestically-produced renewables, concentrating the ecological gains within the EU production system. RoW energy exporters lose export revenues but do not access the domestic ecological efficiency gains that accompany the EU transition. The fiscal dimension is equally extreme: RoW government deficit diverges by −1.31 percentage points (Sc13), because hydrocarbon-exporting governments face revenue collapse. This is a canonical ecologically unequal exchange (EUE) outcome: the core economy (EU) decarbonises at the periphery’s (RoW) fiscal expense.

Why construction (Sc5, Sc14) generates blue. Construction Rebound scenarios are the only cases generating systematically blue ecological cells — specifically in emissions (+5.14 and +2.16 for Sc5 and Sc14 respectively). The rebound is confined to the atmospheric dimension: the land divergences for the same two scenarios are −0.30 and −0.13, and the water divergences −0.03 and −0.01, both negative. This sign reversal in emissions is the defining feature of the “rebound” label: CE policy in construction increases fixed investment (as construction investment is itself the dominant channel), and the EU capital formation surge draws on more energy-intensive renovation activity that pushes EU emissions above RoW levels. The label “Construction Rebound” is therefore correct, but it names a carbon rebound specifically, not a general ecological one.

Production Leakage (Sc1, Sc4, Sc9) shows moderate but consistent red in ecological columns, indicating that EU’s ecological gains exceed RoW’s — but less dramatically than the fossil scenarios. The leakage occurs through intermediate import channels: secondary-sector production in the EU draws more on RoW inputs, partially diffusing the ecological gain outward.

Competitive Displacement (Sc10) stands out uniquely in the macro columns: blue cells for consumption, value added, gross output, and employment indicate that EU outperforms RoW on macroeconomic outcomes. This is the only scenario where a true sign reversal occurs — EU macro variables move positively while RoW contracts — rather than both contracting at different rates. The intensity is moderate, however, making Sc10’s statistical distinctiveness from the Fossil Import Collapse group an open question addressed in Section 5.

4 ANOVA: Are Regime Divergences Statistically Different?

One-way ANOVA tests whether mean EU−RoW divergence differs across the 5 transmission regimes (H₀: all group means equal; df_between = 4, df_within = 9). Effect size η² = SS_between / SS_total is analogous to R². The OLS regression fits Z2 ~ Z1 across the 14 scenarios per variable, where slope > 0 indicates co-movement and slope < 0 indicates asymmetric sign reversal. Both analyses use long-term (t+20 periods) percentage deviations from baseline.

Discussion. Regime membership is a strong predictor of EU−RoW divergence: 30 of 34 variables achieve η² ≥ 0.70. Ecological and fiscal variables lead: material use (mat, η² ≈ 0.98), recycling (rec, η² ≈ 0.97), government bonds (b_s, η² ≈ 0.95), and land/emissions (η² ≈ 0.92–0.94). These are driven by the extreme divergences in the Fossil Import Collapse and Construction Rebound groups.

The OLS slope column reveals the direction of bilateral co-movement. Slopes are negative for consumption, value added, employment, and wealth: as EU contracts, RoW expands (asymmetric). Slopes are strongly positive and near 1.0 for fiscal variables (government deficit, bonds): both regions’ fiscal positions move together, amplified. Ecological variables show positive slopes below 1.0, meaning RoW ecological changes are systematically smaller than EU’s in absolute terms — the ecological gains from CE accrue disproportionately to the EU production system.

Variables with low η² and near-zero slopes — wage share (shw), household loans (lh) — are regime-blind: cross-border transmission in CE scenarios does not systematically affect household financial conditions in RoW, regardless of which regime is operating.

5 Hierarchical Clustering: Two Coordinate Spaces

5.1 Why the coordinate space matters

The five transmission regimes are defined by a pair of regional signs. “Competitive Displacement” is the case where the EU expands while the Rest of World contracts; “Symmetric Contraction” is the case where both move the same way. Those are statements about the joint pattern of Z1 and Z2, not about their difference.

This has a direct consequence for how the scenarios may be clustered. A divergence of +0.5 is produced equally by (Z1 +0.4, Z2 −0.1) — a genuine sign reversal — and by (Z1 +0.6, Z2 +0.1), where both regions expand. Those are two different regimes with identical coordinates. Differencing removes the information the regime taxonomy is defined by, and no clustering algorithm can recover a distinction the coordinate transform has already destroyed.

Two spaces are therefore used throughout what follows, and they answer different questions:

space vector per scenario what it can test
Divergence Z1 − Z2 one value per variable cross-border asymmetry — how unequally a shock lands
Joint (Z1, Z2) two values per variable, standardised separately the full two-region signature, including sign patterns

The divergence space additionally destroys the current account and trade balance outright: cab and tb are bilateral accounting identities that cancel exactly between the regions, so their divergence is identically zero and they are dropped. In the joint space both survive.

5.2 Clustering Procedure

Scenarios are clustered on the 37 documented aggregates, in both spaces: 72 columns in the joint space and 34 in the divergence space. The difference is the three variables whose divergence has zero variance and is therefore dropped — cab and tb, which cancel bilaterally as accounting identities, and g, which is exogenous and identical across scenarios. All three carry information in the joint space and are retained there. Variables are standardised before clustering so that high-variance fiscal variables do not dominate the distance metric.

Algorithm: Ward’s D2 linkage with Euclidean distance. Ward’s method minimises within-cluster total variance at each merge step, producing compact, similarly-sized clusters appropriate for the small sample (n=14).

5.3 Dendrogram

Discussion. The dendrogram reveals three primary splits at the highest level of the hierarchy:

  1. First split separates Sc5 (Cnst-FD) from all other scenarios. This isolation reflects the extreme magnitude of the construction final-demand shock: at ρ=0.05 applied to the dominant investment channel (66.7% of total construction demand, 88.7 billion EUR), Sc5 generates divergence values — particularly in emissions (+5.14) — that are an order of magnitude larger than any other scenario. It is not merely “different in kind” but different in scale.

  2. Second split separates Sc13 (Enrg-Int) from a broader group. Sc13 is the maximum-leverage scenario in the entire set: its intermediate energy channel (14.8 billion EUR, largest in the set) combined with the 3.3:1 intensity differential generates the largest ecological and fiscal divergences after Sc5. Like Sc5, it is an outlier in magnitude within its own regime group.

  3. Third split and below produces the remaining groupings, where the data broadly confirms the paper taxonomy — Production Leakage (Sc1, 4, 9) and Symmetric Contraction (Sc3, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12) cluster together, while Sc10 (Mtl-Int), Sc2 (Enrg-HH), and Sc14 (Cnst-Int) form a middle group with moderate positive EU−RoW macro divergences.

A critical observation from the dendrogram is that Sc10 (Competitive Displacement) does not form an isolated branch — it clusters with Sc2 and Sc14 before joining Sc13. This is a meaningful challenge to its status as a standalone regime and is explored further in Section 4.3.

5.4 How Many Clusters? Silhouette Against a Permutation Null

Three of the four criteria previously reported here — the gap statistic and the AIC and BIC of a Gaussian mixture model — are not usable on this data, and the reason is structural rather than incidental. With 34 variables and 14 scenarios, p/n ≈ 2.4.

  • The gap statistic compares observed within-cluster dispersion against a uniform reference distribution over the bounding box of the data. In 34 dimensions containing 14 points that reference is dispersed almost everywhere, the comparison degenerates, and the 1-SE rule fires at the first k it tests.
  • Gaussian mixture models estimate a mean vector and a covariance structure per component. With p > n the likelihood is not identified, and the reported optimum is the search ceiling rather than an estimate.

They are replaced here by a permutation null, which makes no distributional assumption: each variable’s column is permuted independently, destroying the association between variables within a scenario while preserving every variable’s marginal distribution exactly. The question it answers is the one that matters — is the observed cluster separation greater than what exchangeable data of the same shape produces?

Discussion. Two results, and they must be kept apart.

There is cluster structure, and it is unambiguous. Across 300 permutations the observed silhouette is never matched at any k from 2 to 8, in any of the three variable sets — not one of the 300 draws matched it, so the permutation p-value is below the resolution of the test, 0.0033 (0 exceedances out of 300) — with observed values 3.0 to 11.0 times the null mean. The earlier reading — that a gap statistic and a BIC of k=1 indicated no structure — was wrong: those criteria are uninformative here, not negative.

The number of clusters is not identified. On the pooled variable set silhouette is effectively flat between k=2 and k=3 (a gap of 0.009 in the joint space) and declines gently thereafter without a clear interior maximum. That is the expected behaviour of a relative criterion at n=14 and it is not a defect in the scenario set.

The consequence for this analysis is methodological. Because k is not identified, the five-regime taxonomy cannot be discovered from these data. It can, however, be tested: it is a partition specified in advance on mechanistic grounds, and the question is whether clustering recovers it. That question is answered with the adjusted Rand index (ARI), which counts the scenario pairs two partitions agree about, corrected for chance — 0 is chance-level agreement, 1 is identity.

5.5 Which Variables Carry the Regime Signal?

The regimes are named for transmission mechanisms — Production Leakage, Competitive Displacement, Fossil Import Collapse, Symmetric Contraction, Construction Rebound. None names an ecological outcome. If that naming is more than rhetorical, the regime signal should sit in the variables through which transmission runs, and not in the ecological satellite accounts.

That is testable. Each of the six blocks defined above is clustered on its own, in both spaces, and its partition at the taxonomy’s own k (5) scored against the taxonomy.

Discussion. The blocks differ enormously in what they carry, and the pattern is systematic.

Real activity in the joint space is the only specification whose silhouette selects k=5 (0.607, rising monotonically from k=2), and its partition matches the taxonomy at ARI 0.906.

The External block is the sharpest small block. In the divergence space it retains only two usable variables — imp and rex, once cab and tb have cancelled — and still reaches the highest silhouette in the table (0.717) with ARI 0.843. In the joint space all four survive and ARI rises to 0.872. Cross-border trade flows discriminate the regimes nearly as well as real activity does, on a fraction of the variables.

The Ecological block carries almost no regime information: ARI 0.190 in the divergence space and 0.435 in the joint space, the two lowest figures in the table. This is the substantive finding of the section, not a nuisance result. Transmission regimes are constituted in the trade and real-activity structure; ecological outcomes are consequences of those regimes rather than definitions of them. The regime taxonomy and the ecological results are therefore logically independent, which is what allows the paper to report an ecological trilemma within a regime rather than confounding the two.

The previously published specification — all variables, divergence space — is the second-worst cell in the table (ARI 0.565), beaten only by the two blocks that carry no signal. It pooled a strong real-activity and external signal with an ecological block that has none, and then differenced away the sign patterns the regimes are defined by.

5.6 Does the Data Recover the Five-Regime Taxonomy?

Adjusted Rand index between the data partition and the taxonomy of 5 groups, by k and coordinate space, on the full variable set of 14 scenarios.
Space k=2 k=3 k=4 k=5 k=6
Divergence 0.432 0.449 0.488 0.565 0.586
Joint 0.432 0.449 0.821 0.936 0.867

On the full variable set in the joint space, the k=5 partition matches the taxonomy at ARI 0.936. In the divergence space the same cut reaches only 0.565.

That partition is stable: removing each of the 72 columns in turn and re-clustering gives an adjusted Rand index of 1.000 against the full-set partition in 72 of 72 cases. Bootstrap resampling of the variable set (500 replicates, columns drawn with replacement) gives mean ARI 0.836, with 67% of replicates at or above 0.8.

Two of the 5 regimes are recovered exactly by almost every specification. Production Leakage {Sc1, Sc4, Sc9} and Symmetric Contraction {Sc3, Sc6, Sc7, Sc8, Sc11, Sc12} — 9 of the 14 scenarios — appear with no errors in 9 of the 9 block-and-space combinations scoring at or above ARI 0.8. They are the solid core of the taxonomy.

The disagreements are confined to the five high-leverage scenarios and are systematic, not random. Sc5 (Cnst-FD) is a singleton in every high-ARI partition: it is an outlier in magnitude rather than a regime member. Sc10 (Mtl-Int) never forms its own cluster, attaching to {Sc2, Sc13} in the real-activity and finance blocks and to {Sc14} in the full joint set. Sc14 (Cnst-Int) moves between blocks. These three facts are reported as findings rather than smoothed away; the implications for “Competitive Displacement” as a standalone regime are taken up below.

A caution on variable selection. Drawing random subsets of the pooled divergence variables, silhouette lands on k=5 in roughly one draw in ten and the k=5 partition reaches ARI ≥ 0.9 in about one in four. Searching over subsets until one yields five clusters is therefore not evidence. Two things distinguish the results above from that failure: the six blocks are a pre-existing economic partition of the variables rather than a search, and the reason for expecting real activity and external flows to carry the signal is stated independently of the result. The mean ARI of 0.62–0.66 across random subsets separately shows the taxonomy is legible in almost any slice of these data, so it does not rest on one fortunate specification.

5.7 Cluster Assignments Across k

Discussion. This panel is the most direct comparison between the data-driven structure and the paper taxonomy. Several features stand out:

Stable groupings across all k: Sc3, Sc6, Sc7, Sc8, Sc11, Sc12 (Symmetric Contraction) consistently remain in the same cluster. Sc1, Sc4, Sc9 (Production Leakage) also cohere at k≥3, though Sc1 separates at k=5 due to its larger absolute divergence magnitudes (Food-HH has the largest household-channel size). These two groupings are the most statistically robust elements of the taxonomy.

Sc5 (Cnst-FD) separates first at k=3, confirming it as the strongest outlier in the dataset. No matter how many clusters are requested, Sc5 occupies its own group from k=3 onwards. The construction final-demand rebound is not just a different type of transmission — it is a different order of magnitude.

Sc10, Sc2, Sc14 cluster together across k=2,3,4 before Sc14 splits at k=5 and Sc10 at k=6. This challenges the separate naming of “Competitive Displacement” (Sc10) and “Construction Rebound-Int” (Sc14) as distinct regimes from the Fossil Import Collapse group (Sc2, Sc13). From a divergence-profile perspective, these three scenarios share the same signature: moderate positive EU macro divergence, moderate negative RoW fiscal divergence.

Sc13 (Enrg-Int) remains in the same cluster as Sc5 until k=5, when it finally merges into the Sc10/Sc2/Sc14 group. At k=4, Sc13 forms its own group — the second outlier in magnitude after Sc5.

5.8 Silhouette Plots by k

Discussion. Silhouette plots reveal which specific scenarios are most and least confidently classified at each k. Average silhouette width is 0.460 at k=3, 0.424 at k=4 and 0.394 at k=5.

At k=3, every coefficient is non-negative, and the cut already isolates Sc5 (Cnst-FD) as a singleton, which is why its coefficient is exactly 0. Eight of the fourteen sit above 0.5, all of them in the symmetric-contraction core (Sc3, 6, 8, 12 at 0.66–0.69). The weakest members of the merged high-leverage group are Sc14 (0.17) and Sc2 (0.23), and the weakest scenario that is not a singleton is Sc14 — the construction intermediate scenario that Sc5’s presence forces into the same cluster as the energy scenarios.

At k=4, two scenarios are singletons and so score 0 by definition: Sc1 (Food-HH), which has the largest household channel and is the furthest of the leakage trio from the other two, and Sc5. The Sc10/Sc2/Sc13/Sc14 group stays whole at this k.

At k=5, Sc10’s coefficient turns negative (−0.03), the only negative value in the schedule: cut into {Sc10, Sc14}, it sits closer to another cluster than to its own. That is the sharpest single expression of Sc10’s weak standing on this registry, and it is examined in “On ‘Competitive Displacement’ as a Standalone Regime” below.

7 Discussion of Main Findings

7.1 What the Divergence Space Groups, and What It Cannot

The section below describes the structure the divergence clustering finds. It is a real structure, but it must be read for what it is: a grouping by cross-border asymmetry, not by regime. Three groups appear at k=3 in that space, and they are not the five regimes — they cannot be, because differencing has removed the two-region sign patterns the regimes are defined by (see “Why the coordinate space matters”). The recovery of the taxonomy is reported in “Does the Data Recover the Five-Regime Taxonomy?” above, on the joint profile, at ARI 0.936.

The three asymmetry groups are:

Cluster A — Near-zero bilateral divergence (Sc3, Sc6–Sc9, Sc11–Sc12, plus Sc1/Sc4 at k=3): These scenarios generate proportional bilateral adjustments. The EU restructuring is too small in absolute scale to generate measurable directional asymmetry in any variable category. The paper’s distinction between “Symmetric Contraction” and “Production Leakage” within this cluster is theoretically motivated — the sign of the divergence differs (Production Leakage generates slightly negative divergences, meaning RoW benefits marginally more than EU) — but statistically the difference is within the noise. At k=3 the data confirms this: both regimes occupy the same cluster.

Cluster B — Moderate EU gain, moderate RoW fiscal cost (Sc2, Sc10, Sc14, and at higher k, Sc13): These scenarios share a common divergence signature: EU macro variables outperform RoW (positive divergence in c, va, n), while RoW government deficit diverges negatively (RoW fiscal space contracts). The mechanisms differ across these scenarios — fossil import substitution (Sc2/Sc13), A-matrix row-sum release (Sc10), and intermediate investment restructuring (Sc14) — but their aggregate cross-border profile is indistinguishable at k≤4.

Cluster C — Extreme outliers (Sc5 alone at k=3; Sc5 and Sc13 at k=4): These scenarios are outliers in magnitude, not just direction. Sc5 generates an emission divergence of +5.14; Sc13 generates an emission divergence of −1.53. Both stand apart from all other scenarios not because their mechanism differs qualitatively but because the scale of their shock transmission dwarfs the rest of the scenario set.

One caveat on Sc5’s isolation. Sc5 is run at ρ = 0.05 where the other scenarios use ρ = 0.2, so part of the distance separating it from everything else is a shock-magnitude choice rather than a structural difference in transmission. Its singleton status is robust across every specification tried, but the analysis here cannot separate the two contributions; a re-run at common ρ would settle it.

7.2 On “Competitive Displacement” as a Standalone Regime

The original justification for isolating Sc10 (Mtl-Int) as “Competitive Displacement” rests on a mechanistic distinction: it is the only scenario in the set where EU macro variables move positive while RoW macro variables move negative simultaneously (true sign reversal). In all other high-divergence scenarios, both regions move in the same direction — EU contracts less than RoW, but both contract.

The cluster analysis confirms this intuition is correct in direction but insufficient to justify a separate statistical regime. At every k from 2 to 5, Sc10 clusters with Sc2 (Enrg-HH) and Sc14 (Cnst-Int) — scenarios where EU contracts only marginally and RoW contracts moderately. The difference between “EU slightly positive while RoW slightly negative” (Sc10) and “EU near-zero while RoW slightly negative” (Sc2/Sc14) is too small in the full 37-variable divergence space for the clustering algorithm to separate them.

Recommendation: Maintain “Competitive Displacement” as a labelled mechanism within the broader “EU gains relative to RoW” grouping, noting that Sc10’s sign reversal is the most extreme example of a pattern shared by Sc2, Sc13, and Sc14. Sc10 is the weakest element of the five-regime taxonomy: it never forms its own cluster in any block or space tested, attaching to {Sc2, Sc13} in the real-activity and finance blocks and to {Sc14} on the full joint variable set. The remaining four regimes are well supported — Production Leakage and Symmetric Contraction recovered exactly by seven of the nine specifications scoring above ARI 0.8, and the taxonomy as a whole recovered at ARI 0.936 on the joint profile. The honest statement is therefore that the five-regime taxonomy is a mechanistic hypothesis specified in advance which the data corroborate at k=5, not a partition that any criterion selects unprompted; k is not identified at n=14.

7.3 Why Energy and Construction Dominate

Two structural features of the model explain the extreme salient of the energy (Sc13) and construction (Sc5) scenarios:

Energy (Sc13): The intermediate energy channel is simultaneously the largest channel in the scenario set (14.8 billion EUR) and the most intensity-differential material pair (emission intensity ratio 3.3:1 between secondary and primary energy). These two factors — scale and intensity differential — are multiplicative in the ΔM formula, making Sc13 the highest-leverage ecological scenario by construction. The cross-border fiscal effect is equally extreme because EU fossil fuel imports represent a direct bilateral income transfer: reducing them by ρ=0.2 removes a substantial, concentrated revenue stream from RoW hydrocarbon exporters without any compensating income source within the model’s RoW structure.

Construction (Sc5): The construction channel uniquely operates through investment, not consumption or intermediate demand. The investment multiplier is structurally larger than consumption or intermediate multipliers because investment triggers capital formation, which activates the full capital-investment loop in the SFC model. At ρ=0.05 (lower than the standard ρ=0.2 used for other scenarios), construction still generates the largest absolute divergences because the investment base (88.7 billion EUR, 66.7% of total construction demand) is the largest single channel in the scenario set. The ecological rebound (+5.14 in emissions) occurs because renovation and refurbishment are more energy-intensive per unit of output than new construction in the current A-matrix — the CE intervention increases construction activity, which raises upstream fossil energy demand domestically even as it reduces material throughput per unit. EU land use in Sc5 in fact falls (−0.33% against baseline), so the rebound is atmospheric, not land-based.

7.4 Validity of the Construction Rebound Label

Yes, “Construction Rebound” is precisely the correct label. The term “rebound” in energy and material economics refers to cases where efficiency improvements trigger increased activity that partially or fully offsets the efficiency gain. In Sc5 and Sc14, the CE policy (shifting toward recycled construction materials) lowers the material cost of construction, which — in the SFC investment framework — stimulates additional investment activity. The ecological footprint of this expanded investment (particularly land use) exceeds the material savings from the substitution, producing a net positive EU ecological divergence relative to RoW. This is a structural rebound embedded in the investment linkage, not a modelling artefact.

The label also captures the macroeconomic character of the regime: unlike all other CE scenarios, which generate modest contractionary or near-zero macro effects, construction scenarios generate EU macro expansion (higher employment, value added, output) alongside the ecological rebound. The regime is distinctive in both the macro and ecological dimensions simultaneously.
